# Together AI raises reserved H100 GPU cluster rates

Together AI pricing

Reserved H100: $3.59/hr (7–30d), $3.29 (31–90d), $3.09 (91–180d) Reserved H100: $3.69/hr (7–30d), $3.45 (31–90d), $3.19 (91–180d)

After two cuts in June took reserved H100 down to $3.09/hr, Together has nudged it back up. Every reserved tenor rose by 10–16 cents an hour: 7–30 days to $3.69 (from $3.59), 31–90 days to $3.45 (from $3.29) and 91–180 days to $3.19 (from $3.09).

What it means for buyers. The increase is small, about 3–5%, but it reverses part of the June cuts, which suggests June’s pricing was near the floor for reserved Hopper capacity. On-demand H100 ($3.99/hr) and every H200 and B200 rate held flat, so the gap between committing and paying as you go narrowed: a 7–30 day reservation now saves 7.5% on H100 instead of 10%.

Together AI runs a multi-SKU pure-usage cloud: per-token serverless inference for popular open-weight models (Kimi K3 at $3.00/$15.00, DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 at $1.32/$3.96 with $0.13 cached input, Qwen3.5 9B at $0.17/$0.25, GLM-5.2 at $1.40/$4.40; since 16 October 2026 seven chat models, Kimi K3 among them, can also run on a US-only endpoint at 1.25 times the standard rate, so Kimi K3 costs $3.75/$18.75 there), image generation billed per image or per megapixel (FLUX.2 [dev] $0.0154 per image, FLUX.2 [max] $0.070 per megapixel, SD XL $0.0019 per megapixel), and per-hour dedicated and cluster GPUs. results.title: GPU Cloud Providers: Where to Rent in 2026 | FastGPU
highlights:
As of November 14, 2026, the exact same NVIDIA H100 SXM rents for $1.73 an hour on one platform and $12.29 an hour on another. Same silicon, same 80GB of memory, same throughput, a 7.1x price gap for a physically identical chip. That is not a rounding error or a regional quirk. It is the single most important fact about renting GPUs in 2026, and almost nobody shopping for compute realizes how wide the spread is until they see the two invoices side by side.

...

...

The full price ladder for a single H100 is where to test the two-market structure. An independent survey of more than fifteen providers laid out that ladder earlier in 2026 - IntuitionLabs. Read live as of November 14, 2026, the marketplaces and neoclouds list Vast.ai at $1.73, RunPod Community at $1.99, Lambda at $3.29, and CoreWeave at $6.16, while the hyperscalers list Google Cloud at $5.38, AWS at $6.88, Azure at $6.98, and Oracle at $10.00, for an overall range of $0.98 to $12.29 across every provider listing the card. The shape of that distribution is the tell. If this were one efficient market, prices would cluster tightly around the cost of production. Instead they spread across a 12.5x range, which is exactly what you see when two markets with different pricing logics are reported as if they were one.

...

| Provider | USD per GPU-hour |
| --- | --- |

| CoreWeave | $6.16 |
| AWS | $6.88 |
| Azure | $6.98 |
| Oracle | $10.00 |

Source: FastGPU live H100 prices, each provider's cheapest listed rate

...

The gap is best understood as a multiple. Spheron's 2026 comparison put hyperscalers at roughly three to six times neocloud rates for an identical H100 - Spheron. Read live as of November 14, 2026, Oracle at $10.00 per GPU-hour against Vast.ai at $1.73 is a 5.8x gap, while AWS at $6.88 against Lambda's $3.29 is 2.1x. The important nuance is that the hyperscalers are not all equally expensive, and the order among them moves: the cheapest big-cloud H100 on-demand right now is Google Cloud at $5.38, and Oracle's flat pricing makes it the simplest.

AWS deserves specific credit for moving on price. In June 2025 it announced up to 45% reductions on its NVIDIA GPU instances, including 44% off H100 on-demand, which brought its P5 instance (eight H100s) to $55.04 an hour, or $6.88 per GPU - AWS. That cut made AWS, at the time, the most affordable hyperscaler for on-demand H100 capacity. As of November 14, 2026 it lists $6.88 per GPU, against $5.38 for the cheapest hyperscaler ( Google Cloud) and 3.5x the $1.99 a lean neocloud like Voltage Park charges. Its P6 instances bring B200 capacity at $14.24 per GPU, and the whole offering sits inside the deepest cloud ecosystem in existence, with EFA networking and Savings Plans for committed spend. For a company already running on AWS, keeping GPU workloads in the same account, under the same security and billing, is worth the premium in a way a spreadsheet does not fully capture.

Google Cloud takes a different tack, pairing its on-demand rate with deep spot discounts. Its A3 instance lists an H100 at $5.38 per GPU-hour on-demand as of November 14, 2026, but Spot capacity drops that sharply, and Google advertises spot discounts of up to 91% off default prices for many GPU types - Thunder Compute. That makes GCP a two-faced proposition: 3.1x the market floor ( $1.73) if you need guaranteed on-demand capacity, far cheaper if your workload can ride preemptible instances. Combined with Vertex AI, GKE, and a TPU alternative for teams whose frameworks support it, GCP is the hyperscaler for organizations that can architect around spot and want the tightest integration with a managed ML platform.

Oracle has quietly set itself apart among the hyperscalers through radical simplicity. As of November 14, 2026 it charges a flat $10.00 per GPU-hour for an H100 and $10.00 for an H200, its far more capable sibling with 141GB of memory, a difference of +0% - Spheron. That flat, no-tiers pricing on bare metal with RDMA cluster networking makes Oracle the easiest hyperscaler to reason about, and paying no more for an H200 than an H100 is a genuine bargain if you need the extra memory. Oracle has also pushed hard into scale, reaching general availability on some of the largest H200 superclusters in any cloud. Azure, by contrast, lists its H100 at $6.98 per GPU-hour on-demand, above the cheapest big-cloud rate of $5.38, and its case rests almost entirely on Microsoft and OpenAI stack integration rather than price - Spheron. For an enterprise standardized on Microsoft, that integration is the whole point, and for everyone else, Azure is the tier's cautionary tale about paying for a wrapper you do not need.

...

The synthesis of these forces is a market with a strong secular downtrend and sharp short-term swings, and that combination is precisely why point-in-time comparison pays off. The long arc is down: H100 on-demand fell from around $8 an hour in 2023 to $1.80 to $3.50 by 2026 as lead times collapsed from over a year to a few weeks - presenc.ai. But the short-term reality is jumpy: H100 rents rose 10% in four weeks over the 2025 year-end training crunch, and a separate run-up of around 40% hit between October 2025 and March 2026 on inference demand and memory shortages - Silicon Data.

results.title: Render's Bandwidth Shock Meets Fly.io's GPU Cutoff: What August 1, 2026 Means for EU Developers Choosing a PaaS — sota.io Blog
highlights:
Two unrelated US platform-as-a-service providers are changing what you get for your money on the exact same day. On August 1, 2026, any Render workspace still sitting on a legacy plan auto-migrates to a new plan with dramatically less included bandwidth and a new per-gigabyte overage charge. On the same date, Fly.io's GPU Machines become permanently unavailable, with no in-platform replacement. Neither company coordinated with the other — this is coincidence, not conspiracy — but if you're running production traffic on either platform, the ... Here's exactly what changes, verified against both companies' own documentation, and what to do before the weekend.

...

| Workspace plan | Legacy bandwidth included | New bandwidth included (Aug 1) | Overage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hobby (free) | 100 GB | 5 GB | $0.15 / GB |
| Pro | 500 GB | 25 GB | $0.15 / GB |
| Scale | 1 TB | 1 TB (unchanged) | $0.15 / GB |

...

## Fly.io: GPUs are not being downgraded, they're being switched off

Fly.io's change is smaller in scope but has zero middle ground. Its own pricing documentation states it flatly: "GPUs are deprecated and will be unavailable after August 1." No downgrade tier, no reduced-capacity fallback — GPU Machines stop existing on the platform.

This is a real reversal, not a quiet feature sunset. In a February 2025 blog post, Fly.io had explicitly reassured GPU users it wasn't abandoning the offering, while conceding the business case was hard: "developers don't want GPUs. They don't even want AI/ML models. They want LLMs" — most developers call an API rather than run their own inference, which made Fly's GPU Machines a niche product relative to the engineering investment (the post describes wrestling with Nvidia driver compatibility inside Fly's container-based virtualization stack). Eighteen months later, that niche-market problem apparently won: GPUs are gone entirely.

While they're still live, current GPU pricing on Fly.io is:

| GPU type | Hourly rate |
| --- | --- |
| A10 | $0.75/hr |
| L40S | $0.70/hr |
| A100 40GB PCIe | $1.25/hr |
| A100 80GB SXM | $1.50/hr |

Worth flagging: Fly.io's own community forum has a thread (started February 2026, unresolved as of this writing) from a developer who says the deprecation email they received from Fly.io cited July 31, 2026 — one day earlier than the "after August 1" language in the official docs. Treat July 31 as the operative deadline if you're running anything GPU-dependent on Fly.io; a day of slack you didn't plan for is better than a day of downtime you didn't expect. More importantly, that same thread has no official Fly.io reply with a migration path — the only suggestions come from other community members pointing at RunPod, Modal, and Google Cloud Run. If you're running fine-tuning jobs, local inference, Whisper transcription, or image-generation workloads on Fly GPU Machines, there is no in-platform successor. You are choosing a new GPU provider, full stop, and you have roughly 72 hours to have picked one.

results.title: Choosing a GPU Cloud: Hyperscaler vs Specialist GPU Cloud vs Serverless Inference | School of Web
highlights:
Once you have decided to grab GPUs directly (see the break-even math), the next question is where to rent them. The same H100 runs 2〜5x apart in hourly rate depending on where you rent it. The conclusion up front: if your infrastructure already lives in AWS and integration and regulation matter, go hyperscaler; if pure GPU cost is the goal, a specialist GPU cloud; if you would rather not manage GPUs at all, serverless inference. The GPU server’s structure is covered in What Makes a GPU Server Different; this post is the choice of where to source that GPU. Prices are as of mid-2026.

### Three branches: differing management levels #

GPU sourcing splits into three branches by management level.

- Hyperscalers (AWS, GCP, Azure): GPU instances (AWS P5 and so on) used inside the same account, network, and IAM as your other cloud resources. H100 per-GPU on-demand runs $4〜8 an hour at hyperscalers, and AWS P5 is about $3.9 per GPU after a mid-2025 cut.
- Specialist GPU clouds (Lambda, RunPod, CoreWeave, and others): providers specialized in GPU rental. H100 runs $2〜3.3 on-demand (RunPod PCIe $1.99, Lambda $3.29), and $1〜2 on spot — the same GPU 2〜5x cheaper than a hyperscaler.
- Serverless inference (Together, Fireworks, and others): not renting a GPU but paying per token for model inference. Call open models at $0.05〜7 per million tokens (usually $0.27〜3), with no GPU provisioning or management at all.

There is one way to read it: moving left adds integration and management and raises the price; moving right approaches pure GPU cost but adds things you must handle yourself.

...

Hyperscalers cost several times more than specialist GPU clouds not because the GPU differs (it is the same H100) but because of what is bundled into the price. Hyperscaler rates fold in VPC networking within the same account, IAM, low-latency integration with other managed services (S3, RDS), and enterprise SLA and compliance. Specialist clouds strip that integration and focus on the GPU itself to lower cost.

So the decision narrows to “do you need that integration?” If training data already sits in S3 and the pipeline lives in AWS, the transfer cost, latency, and security review of pulling data out can offset a specialist cloud’s savings. Conversely, for experiments, training, or batch that need only an independent GPU, the specialist cloud’s cost advantage stands as-is.

...

Both specialist GPU clouds and hyperscalers offer spot (interruptible) rates. H100 spot drops to $1〜2 — below half of on-demand. The price is that it can be reclaimed at any time.

- Fitting workloads: training that checkpoints as it runs, batch inference that resumes after interruption, and reproducible experiments. If reclaimed, grab another and continue.
- Misfitting workloads: production inference endpoints that must respond continuously. If the GPU is reclaimed mid-request, the service breaks.

results.title: How to Launch a GPU as a Service Business with vCluster
highlights:
To make the business tangible, here's a snapshot of representative on-demand GPU pricing (rates vary by provider and availability):

| GPU Model | Representative On-Demand Price |
| --- | --- |
| H100 SXM5 | ~$2.50/hr |
| A100 80G SXM4 | ~$1.07/hr |
| B200 SXM6 | ~$6.02/hr |

A 30-GPU cluster of A100s, well-utilized, is a meaningful revenue stream. Getting provisioning right is what makes utilization possible.

...

Common pricing models your tenants will expect:

- On-Demand: Pay-as-you-go, billed by the hour or minute.
- Reserved Capacity: Discounted rates for long-term commitments.
- Spot Pricing: Access to unused capacity at steep discounts for fault-tolerant batch jobs.
